terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Run your file here to read the sign-out book, count days since a check and write report lines.

tasks.title: When it went out
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 1` in `kit_dates.py`, write the line that imports what this file needs from the `datetime` module: Tasks 2 and 3 need more of it than this task does. Then write a function called `out_time` that takes a time from the sign-out book, as text written day/month/year hours:minutes, and gives back a `datetime` with that date and time. For `signed_out` it prints as `2026-03-14 22:40:00`. Print what it gives back for `signed_out`.

Check calls `out_time` with times of its own, one on a day after the 12th of a month, and looks at the `datetime` it gives back.
nextSteps: Read the parts of the lesson on the datetime module and on reading a date from text.
Write the import line, then the def line of out_time.
Write the format that matches the sign-out book, one code for each part, with the / and : in their places.
Print what out_time gives back for signed_out, and compare it with the text.
hints: The module is called `datetime`, and so is one of the types inside it. Which one a name stands for depends on how you imported it.
The type `datetime` has a method that reads a date and time from text, given a format where `%d`, `%m`, `%Y`, `%H` and `%M` stand for the day, month, four-digit year, hour and minute.
The shape is `from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta` at the top of Task 1, and `return datetime.strptime(text, "%d/%m/%Y %H:%M")` inside `out_time`.

tasks.title: Days since the last check
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 2`, write a function called `days_since` that takes the date of a last check, as text written year-month-day, and today, a `date`, and gives back how many days have passed since the check, a whole number. Never read today from the computer's clock: use the date it is given. For `last_check` and `date(2026, 3, 14)` it gives back `64`. Print what it gives back for `last_check` and `date(2026, 3, 14)`.

Check calls `days_since` with dates of its own, far from today, across a new year and a leap day, and looks at what it gives back and whether it read the computer's clock.
nextSteps: Read the parts of the lesson on reading a date from text and on the gap between two dates.
Turn the text of the check into a date.
Take the date of the check from today, and print what you get.
Give back the number of days in it.
hints: Text and a date cannot be taken one from another. Text written year-month-day is the one form `date` can read by itself.
The type `date` has a method that reads text written year-month-day. One date taken from another gives a `timedelta`, which holds its whole number of days.

tasks.title: When the next check is due
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 3`, write a function called `next_check` that takes the year, the month and the day of a check, three whole numbers, and how many days until the next check, and gives back the date of the next check, a `date`. For `2026, 1, 9` and `90` it gives back `date(2026, 4, 9)`. Print what it gives back for `2026, 1, 9` and `90`.

Check calls `next_check` with dates and days of its own, into a new year, a short month and across a leap day, and looks at the `date` it gives back.
nextSteps: Read the parts of the lesson on making a date from its parts and on adding days.
Make the date of the check from the three numbers.
Add the days to it as a timedelta.
Give back the date you get, and print it.
hints: Adding to the day of the month by hand makes days that do not exist, such as the 40th of January. Let the date do the counting.
A date is made from its parts, biggest first, and a gap of some days is a `timedelta`. A date plus a gap is a date.
The shape is `return date(year, month, day) + timedelta(days=every)`.

tasks.title: A line for the report
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 4`, write a function called `report_line` that takes a `datetime` and gives back a text such as `"Saturday 14 March 2026, 22:40"`: the day of the week from `DAYS`, a space, the day of the month with no 0 in front, a space, the month from `MONTHS`, a space, the year, a comma and a space, and the time as hours and minutes, each two digits, with a colon between. Print what it gives back for `out_time(signed_out)`.

Check calls `report_line` with datetimes of its own, early and late in a month and on different days of the week, and looks at the text it gives back.
nextSteps: Read the parts of the lesson on the day of the week and on writing a date for a report.
Find the day of the week as a number, and use it to pick from DAYS.
Pick the month from MONTHS the same way, minding where each count starts.
Put the parts together in an f-string, and compare it with the example.
hints: A datetime has `.day`, `.month`, `.year`, `.hour` and `.minute`, each a number, and a method that gives the day of the week as a number.

A datetime has a method that gives the day of the week counting Monday as 0, which matches the order of `DAYS`. `.month` counts January as 1, and a list counts from 0. In an f-string, a format after a colon writes the hours and minutes with two digits each.
